dashboard.infoSignalPanel: Four independent models assess market conditions from different angles: historical valuation (CAPE), recession risk, market regime, and duration of the current phase. Each model uses different data — a shared signal across models is more reliable than any single indicator.
dashboard.infoRegime: The HMM (Hidden Markov Model) analyses 145 years of market history (Shiller data 1871–2026), automatically finding 4 recurring patterns: bull (cheap stocks, rising), consolidation (cheap, no trend), expensive market (high CAPE, compressed equity risk premium, low expected returns), bear (falling). The model does not know in advance what these patterns mean — labels were assigned by examining each cluster's characteristics. Note: CAPE=39 is well above the cluster centroid (~20), so the model is extrapolating outside its training range.
dashboard.infoRegimeDuration: Measures how long the current market phase has lasted and compares to history. The Kaplan-Meier method (used in medical survival analysis) calculates the probability that a given regime is still ongoing after X months — analogous to radioactive decay half-lives in physics. Current 'expensive market' regime (73 months) is well above the historical median (19 months) — we are in the tail of the distribution.
dashboard.infoDiversification: The diversification index measures how independently assets move from each other. Computed via PCA (Principal Component Analysis) — the same technique as EOF analysis in meteorology. A value of 60% means only 40% of variability can be explained by a single market factor. Higher index = diversification more effectively reduces risk.
dashboard.infoMacro: Raw macroeconomic data fetched daily from official sources (FRED, ECB, NBP). VIX is the 'fear index' — measures expected S&P 500 volatility. HY spread measures extra yield on junk bonds vs government — a high spread signals credit stress. An inverted yield curve (10Y < 3M) has historically preceded recessions.
dashboard.infoVol: The HAR-RV model forecasts VWCE.DE volatility 21 days ahead using historical volatility at multiple time windows (1d, 5d, 21d, 63d) as predictors. Volatility above 25% annualised suggests DCA over a lump sum.
dashboard.infoFX: A LightGBM model forecasts USD/PLN 21 days ahead in three scenarios: optimistic (10th pct), baseline (median), pessimistic (90th pct). Note: forecasting exchange rate direction beyond 3 weeks is very difficult — the median is mainly for assessing FX risk (band width), not as a precise directional forecast.

signals.infoHmm: A statistical model (HMM) analyses 145 years of market history (Shiller data 1871–2026), finding recurring patterns. Inputs: monthly S&P 500 returns, volatility, CAPE (cyclically adjusted P/E), inflation, 10-year bond yield. The model found 4 patterns — 'expensive market' cluster = high CAPE + compressed equity risk premium (negative excess yield) + elevated vol; historical return ~+2%/yr vs ~+7% for bull. The label is NOT classical stagflation (high inflation + stagnation) — it describes an expensive, low-expected-return market environment. Note: CAPE=39 is beyond the cluster's training range (~20 centroid) — assignment carries high uncertainty.
signals.infoRd: Measures how many months the current market phase has lasted vs history. The Kaplan-Meier method (used in medical survival research) calculates the probability that a given phase is still ongoing after X months — analogous to radioactive half-life distributions in physics. Based on 145 years of HMM forecasts. The current 'expensive market' episode (73 months) is far above the historical median (19 months) — we are in the tail of the distribution.
signals.infoRecession: A LightGBM model computes the probability of US recession using leading indicators: yield curve slope (10Y–3M spread), VIX, unemployment, Fed rate, inflation. Trained on official NBER recession dates (1960–2024). Limitation: NBER declares recessions with significant delay (up to a year), so the model may have learned to recognise recessions after the fact. 0% risk means no indicator currently signals an active US recession.
signals.infoCape: CAPE (Cyclically Adjusted P/E) is the stock price divided by 10-year average earnings, smoothing out business cycle fluctuations. Developed by Prof. Robert Shiller (Nobel Prize 2013). Data: 145 years of S&P 500 history (Shiller 1871–2026). The model estimates expected 10-year real return based on current CAPE. CAPE=39 is ~90th historical percentile — stocks were more expensive only ~10% of the time. Limitation: CAPE does not account for earnings growth — if margins and profits have permanently increased (e.g. through AI/technology), historical comparisons may be overly pessimistic.
signals.infoValuation: Global CAPE = 60% US CAPE + 40% estimated ex-US CAPE (~15; Developed ex-US ~16, EM ~13, per Research Affiliates 2024). VWCE is a global fund, so US CAPE (39) overstates risk — after including cheaper European and EM markets the portfolio CAPE drops to ~29. Trailing P/E (32) is lower than CAPE because CAPE uses 10-year averaged earnings including COVID (2020). The 5Y EPS growth rate (+9.7%/yr) exceeds the historical median (6.3%/yr); if driven by structural changes (AI, margins), CAPE may be too pessimistic.

decision.title: Monthly Recommendation
decision.mlHint: Make sure the backend is running and ML models are trained.
decision.horizonNote: Weights vary by horizon: momentum dominates at 1–3Y, CAPE at 2–10Y, base rate at 10Y+.
decision.disclaimer: Projection based on three signals: CAPE valuation (Asness/AQR 2012), global historical equity return (Dimson-Marsh-Staunton 2025, 1900–2024 data), and momentum adjustment from live data. Real returns — inflation not included. Not financial advice.
decision.disclaimerEarnings: Important limitation: all models in this app rely on historical valuation and macroeconomic data. They do not account for earnings growth. If AI, technology, or other factors have permanently raised corporate margins and profits (as in 2020–2026), historical CAPE comparisons may overstate risk. A CAPE of 39 may be justified if earnings have structurally increased — this is something the models cannot see.
